name: Chain-Reaction Lab
topics_techniques_covered: systems_causal_reasoning: 2D physics sandbox where the child places ramps, dominoes, springs and see-saws so one action triggers a chain of effects that guides a ball to a goal
systems_reasoning: the child must reason about how several interacting parts behave together as one machine, not in isolation
mechanical_systems_reasoning: levers, ramps and springboards transmit force/motion; the child predicts and exploits those mechanical effects
problem_solving: open constraint-satisfaction goal (get the ball to the balloon) solved by planning, building, testing and revising
one_liner: The child drops ramps, springs and dominoes into a physics sandbox so a chain reaction rolls the ball into the balloon.
interaction: A ball, some fixed pegs and a goal balloon sit in a play area with a tray of parts (ramp, springboard, domino) below. The child taps a part then taps an empty spot to place it (tap a placed part to pick it up and move or remove it), then taps the big GO button to run the physics and watch the chain reaction. If the ball misses, they adjust parts and run again. No typing, no reading.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand picks a ramp from the tray, drops it under the ball, taps GO, and the ball rolls down the ramp into the balloon which pops with confetti - under 10s. One unscored warm-up level (one gap to bridge with a single ramp) runs next, giving a happy pop for success or a gentle reset if the ball misses, before scored levels begin.

learning_science.why: Embedding measurement inside sandbox play removes test anxiety and captures the reasoning process, not just the outcome.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Every placement, run and revision is logged as evidence and scored against a causal-reasoning model rather than only pass/fail on the final run.
learning_science.source: Shute, V. J. (2011). Stealth assessment in computer-based games to support learning. In Tobias & Fletcher (Eds.), Computer Games and Instruction.

learning_science.why: Newton's-Playground-style sandboxes validly elicit intuitive physics and problem-solving talent.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Levels are designed around agents of force (ramps, springs, pendulums, levers) so success depends on causal physical reasoning, echoing the validated Newton's Playground design.
learning_science.source: Shute, V. J., Ventura, M., & Kim, Y. J. (2013). Assessment and learning of qualitative physics in Newton's Playground. Journal of Educational Research 106(6).

tail_precision_rationale: M-EFF (parts and reruns used versus the optimal solution) and M-HYP (how quickly each test rules out failing configurations) separate strong causal reasoners who plan an efficient machine from trial-and-error builders even when both eventually solve the level. M-RTFIRST captures the reflective planning pause before the first placement that marks able solvers, while M-PATH and M-EXPLORE preserve the full build sequence for evidence-model scoring, and M-PERSIST on hard levels adds a task-commitment signal at the tail.
age_rationale: Tap-to-place with large snap targets removes fine-motor drawing demands, so children from 2-3 can build. 2-3 gets one-gap levels with a single part type; 4-5 adds springs and multiple parts; 6-8 adds pendulums, chained triggers and tight part budgets that require multi-step causal foresight. Pre-literacy is fine because all instruction is the wordless ghost-hand.

adaptive.content_range: one-ramp single-gap levels (2-3) up to multi-part chained-trigger contraptions under a strict part budget (6-8 tail)
difficulty_levers: number of interacting parts and triggers
presence of dynamic elements (pendulum, spring timing)
adaptive.notes: Levels are procedurally generable by sampling obstacle layouts and part budgets; the physics engine auto-verifies solvability and optimal part count for M-EFF.

engagement_hook: Building a Rube-Goldberg chain reaction and watching dominoes topple and the balloon pop is intrinsically playful, and tighter part budgets feel like unlocking harder puzzle levels.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Guard motor load with tap-to-place snapping (no precision dragging); keep the physics predictable so outcomes reflect reasoning not chaotic luck; the ghost-hand plus warm-up neutralises game-novelty variance; do not reward raw speed since reflective builders take longer before the first placement; ensure parts are distinguishable by shape not colour alone.

name: Gearworks
topics_techniques_covered: mechanical_systems_reasoning: the child connects gears, belts and pulleys so the final wheel turns the required direction and relative speed
systems_reasoning: meshed gears form one coupled system; the child reasons about how a change to one part propagates through the whole train
systems_causal_reasoning: turning the crank causes a chain of rotations; the child predicts the causal outcome at the end of the train
inductive_reasoning: the child infers the hidden meshing/ratio rule (direction flips each mesh; speed scales with teeth) from watching examples
problem_solving: reach a target rotation with a limited set of gears, a constraint-satisfaction design task
one_liner: The child drops gears onto pegs to build a working gear train that spins the flag the right way and speed.
interaction: A driver crank on the left and a target flag-wheel on the right sit on a pegboard with a tray of gears (small/medium/large) and belts below. The child taps a gear then taps a peg to mount it so it meshes with its neighbour, links two far wheels with a belt by tapping both, then taps GO to spin the crank and see whether the flag turns the shown direction (and reaches the shown speed). Tap a mounted gear to remove it. No typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand mounts one gear between the crank and the flag, taps GO, and the whole train spins so the flag waves - under 10s, showing that meshing gears transmit motion. One unscored warm-up (mesh a single gear to make the flag turn at all) gives spinning-gear success feedback or a gentle nudge, before scored direction/speed targets begin.

learning_science.why: People reason about pulleys and gears by mentally animating the components, and expertise shows as chunked rule use (direction alternation, ratio scaling).
learning_science.concrete_decision: The train animates on GO so children can run and inspect their mental model, and difficulty rises by adding meshes and ratio demands that reward rule-based over step-by-step simulation.
learning_science.source: Hegarty, M. (1992). Mental animation: Inferring motion from static displays of mechanical systems. Journal of Experimental Psychology: LMC 18(5).

learning_science.why: Process telemetry from an open build separates how a child reasons from whether the final train works.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Each mount, belt link and rerun is logged and scored against a mechanical-reasoning evidence model, not just the final direction check.
learning_science.source: Mislevy, R. J., Almond, R. G., & Lukas, J. F. (2003). A brief introduction to evidence-centered design. ETS Research Report RR-03-16.

tail_precision_rationale: M-EFF (gears used versus the minimal train) and M-ERRTYPE (a direction-only miss versus a speed-ratio miss versus a broken mesh) resolve near-misses into the specific mechanical rule a child has or lacks, sharpening placement just below the cut. M-HYP indexes whether reruns are disambiguating tests of the ratio rule versus random swaps, and M-RTFIRST credits the reflective planning of the train before the first mount that marks strong mechanical reasoners.
age_rationale: Understanding that meshing gears alternate direction and that size changes speed needs some proportional intuition, so 4-5 starts at direction-only single-mesh targets with large snap pegs, and 6-8 adds multi-gear trains, belt drives and speed-ratio targets that demand multiplicative reasoning. Below 4-5 the ratio concept is generally inaccessible, setting the lower bound.

adaptive.content_range: single-mesh make-it-turn targets (4-5) up to multi-stage trains with belts and exact speed-ratio and direction targets (6-8 tail)
difficulty_levers: number of meshes in the train
adaptive.notes: Trains and targets are procedurally sampled with an auto-solver computing the minimal gear count and the exact output ratio, giving keys for M-EFF and M-ACC and unlimited parallel clones.

engagement_hook: Snapping gears together and watching the whole machine whir to life and wave a flag gives immediate mechanical satisfaction, and speed-ratio targets feel like tuning a real machine.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Guard fine-motor load with snap-to-peg placement; distinguish gear sizes by silhouette not colour; keep the animation legible so the direction/speed outcome is unambiguous; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; avoid rewarding fast guessing by crediting efficient minimal trains over rapid gear-spamming.

name: Critter Gates
topics_techniques_covered: inductive_reasoning: the child infers a hidden attribute rule from feedback and routes creatures through the gate that accepts them (Zoombinis-style rule induction)
problem_solving: reach the goal of getting every creature through by decomposing attributes and testing hypotheses
systems_reasoning: multiple attribute dimensions (colour, shape, feet) interact to define the hidden rule the child must coordinate
one_liner: The child sends each little creature to the left or right gate to discover, from accept/reject feedback, the hidden rule about which creatures each gate lets pass.
interaction: A creature appears with visible attributes (body colour, shape, number of feet). Two gates are shown. The child taps the left or right gate to send the creature there; the gate flashes green (passed) or bounces it back (rejected). Over successive creatures the child uses the feedback to work out the rule, aiming to route each new creature correctly on the first try. No typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand takes a red creature, sends it to the left gate which flashes green, then takes a blue creature and sends it right which flashes green - under 10s, showing that different creatures belong to different gates and feedback tells you if you were right. One unscored warm-up round on an obvious one-attribute rule (colour) runs before the scored, harder rules begin.

learning_science.why: Rule discovery is a coordinated search of a hypothesis space and an experiment space; able reasoners run informative tests and revise hypotheses efficiently.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Feedback-bearing placements let us measure whether each routing choice is a maximally disambiguating experiment or a redundant guess, indexing hypothesis-search quality.
learning_science.source: Klahr, D., & Dunbar, K. (1988). Dual space search during scientific reasoning. Cognitive Science 12(1).

learning_science.principle: Concept attainment from positive and negative instances
learning_science.why: Inferring a category rule from labelled examples is a classic marker of inductive reasoning and strategy (focusing versus scanning).
learning_science.concrete_decision: Gates give clean positive/negative feedback per attribute-combination so the child's strategy (systematic focusing versus haphazard scanning) is observable and scorable.
learning_science.source: Bruner, J. S., Goodnow, J. J., & Austin, G. A. (1956). A Study of Thinking. Wiley.

tail_precision_rationale: M-HYP (viable-rule-space reduction per routing) and M-EFF (trials to reach the criterion of error-free routing) are the sharpest separators: strong inducers converge on the rule in few, well-chosen tests while others perseverate or guess. M-RULEID captures how many interacting attribute dimensions the rule combines (one to three), so the ceiling probes relational complexity, and M-ACC on the first post-inference trials confirms the rule was truly abstracted rather than memorised.
age_rationale: Sorting by a single obvious attribute with immediate feedback is accessible to K-1 with large tap targets and no reading. Difficulty scales purely by rule complexity: 2-3 single-attribute rules, 4-5 two-attribute conjunctions, 6-8 disjunctive or three-attribute rules, so one shell spans all bands without any literacy or motor precision demand.

adaptive.content_range: single-attribute colour rules (K-1) up to three-attribute conjunctive/disjunctive rules requiring several disambiguating tests (6-8 tail)
adaptive.notes: Rules are generated from an attribute grammar with the viable-hypothesis set computed after each trial for M-HYP; endless parallel forms and above-level rules support ceiling probing.

engagement_hook: Cracking a secret rule from clues is a mystery-solving hook, and each newly discovered gate rule feels like levelling up a detective.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Attributes are shape/feet/pattern coded, not colour-only, for colour-vision fairness; large gate tap targets remove motor demands; feedback is immediate and wordless to avoid reading load; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; scoring credits efficient rule inference over lucky early guesses via M-HYP and the post-criterion accuracy check.

name: Gem Trail
topics_techniques_covered: spatial_navigation: the child plans and traces a route through a maze/world to collect gems and reach the exit (virtual navigation assessment)
planning_lookahead: the route must be planned ahead to avoid dead-ends and minimise backtracking
problem_solving: find an efficient path satisfying pick-up-all-gems-then-exit constraints
one_liner: The child taps a path through a maze to collect all the gems and reach the door using as few steps as possible.
interaction: A top-down maze shows a start avatar, gems, walls and an exit door. The child taps an adjacent open cell (or drags along a corridor) to move the avatar step by step; the trail is drawn behind them. Tapping backward retraces. When all gems are collected and the avatar reaches the door the level completes. No typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand taps three cells in a row from the avatar to a gem to the door; the avatar glides along and the door opens - under 10s. One unscored warm-up on a tiny 3x3 maze with one gem runs, celebrating arrival or gently showing the path, before scored mazes begin.

learning_science.why: Efficient navigation reflects building and using a spatial representation, a distinct large-scale spatial ability.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Mazes require integrating a route over the whole layout (gems plus exit) rather than a single straight path, so route efficiency indexes cognitive-map use.
learning_science.source: Tolman, E. C. (1948). Cognitive maps in rats and men. Psychological Review 55(4).

learning_science.principle: Planning measured by look-ahead before acting
learning_science.why: Strong planners think ahead and commit fewer wasted moves; first-move latency and moves-over-optimal expose planning quality.
learning_science.concrete_decision: We log the pause before the first move and moves versus the shortest gem-collecting route so planful navigation is distinguished from reactive wandering.
learning_science.source: Shallice, T. (1982). Specific impairments of planning. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B 298(1089).

tail_precision_rationale: M-EFF (steps taken versus the optimal all-gem route) is a continuous, ceiling-resistant separator: strong navigators approach the optimum while others wander. M-RTFIRST captures pre-move planning (able children study the maze before starting) and M-REV/M-EXPLORE distinguish decisive routing from repeated backtracking, turning one solved maze into a graded route-quality estimate rather than a solved/unsolved bit.
age_rationale: Tap-to-move on a grid with big cells is accessible from 2-3 on small mazes with one gem. 4-5 adds more gems and branch points; 6-8 uses dense mazes with many blind alleys and required gem ordering that demand route optimisation and look-ahead. Grids avoid fine-motor drawing and there is no reading.

adaptive.content_range: 3x3 one-gem mazes (2-3) up to dense multi-gem mazes with many dead-ends and ordering constraints (6-8 tail)
difficulty_levers: number of gems and whether an order is forced
number and depth of blind alleys
presence of one-way or toll cells
optional step budget for a star rating
adaptive.notes: Mazes are procedurally generated with a solver computing the optimal gem-collecting path length for M-EFF; unlimited parallel forms and above-level mazes for ceiling probing.

engagement_hook: Collecting sparkling gems and finding the secret shortest path is a classic treasure-hunt hook, with star ratings for efficient routes driving replay.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Large grid cells remove motor-precision demands; the whole maze is visible so it measures planning not memory; walls are high-contrast for low-vision access; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; efficiency (not speed) is scored so deliberate planners are not penalised for pausing to think.

name: Slide & Stack
topics_techniques_covered: manipulation: the child mentally and physically manipulates blocks - sliding and rotating pieces to free a path or pack a crate
planning_lookahead: freeing the key block or packing without gaps requires ordering moves several steps ahead
problem_solving: a spatial constraint-satisfaction goal (clear the exit / fill the crate) with limited moves
one_liner: The child slides blocks out of the way so the special block can reach the exit, packing the space with as few moves as possible.
interaction: A grid holds a target block and several obstacle blocks (sliding-block puzzle). The child taps a block then taps the direction/empty space to slide it as far as it can go; the goal is to open a clear lane so the target block slides off the exit edge. A move counter shows moves used. Tap-undo reverts the last slide. No typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand taps an obstacle block, slides it aside, then slides the target block out through the opened exit - under 10s. One unscored warm-up with a single obstacle runs, celebrating the exit or gently resetting, before scored configurations begin.

learning_science.principle: Spatial ability is malleable and manipulation is a core factor
learning_science.why: Object-manipulation tasks (mental rotation, transformation) form a trainable, STEM-predictive spatial factor distinct from static reasoning.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The task requires manipulating and reordering pieces under constraints, targeting the manipulation factor rather than passive pattern recognition.
learning_science.source: Uttal, D. H., et al. (2013). The malleability of spatial skills: A meta-analysis of training studies. Psychological Bulletin 139(2).

learning_science.why: Sliding-block puzzles require setting sub-goals (move A to later move B), a hallmark of planful problem solving.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Move-count and moves-over-minimum are scored so decomposing the puzzle into sub-goals is credited over blind sliding.
learning_science.source: Newell, A., & Simon, H. A. (1972). Human Problem Solving. Prentice-Hall.

tail_precision_rationale: M-EFF (moves versus the minimum solution) is a fine continuous discriminator that resists ceiling on hard configurations, and M-RTFIRST captures the planning pause that precedes efficient solutions. M-REV and M-EXPLORE separate confident planned sequences from guess-and-check sliding, while M-PROG turns a single hard puzzle into a solve-trajectory curve that adds tail resolution beyond solved/unsolved.
age_rationale: Tap-a-block-then-tap-a-direction sliding with large cells is accessible from 2-3 on 3x3 single-obstacle boards. 4-5 adds more obstacles; 6-8 uses larger boards with interlocking blocks and tight move budgets that demand multi-step manipulation and look-ahead. No reading and no precise dragging are required.

adaptive.content_range: single-obstacle 3x3 boards (2-3) up to dense interlocking boards with minimal move budgets (6-8 tail)
difficulty_levers: number and size of obstacle blocks
number of blocks that must move before the target
optional move budget for a star rating
adaptive.notes: Configurations are generated and a breadth-first solver stores the minimum move count for M-EFF; unlimited parallel forms and deeper above-level boards for ceiling probing.

engagement_hook: The satisfying click of blocks sliding into place and freeing the trapped block is a well-loved puzzle mechanic, with fewest-moves stars rewarding elegant solutions.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Tap-then-direction sliding removes precise-drag motor demands; blocks are shape/pattern distinct for colour-vision fairness; the full board is visible so it taxes manipulation not memory; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; scoring rewards move efficiency over speed so reflective solvers are not penalised.

name: Portal Planner
topics_techniques_covered: planning_lookahead: the child rearranges orbs across pegs to match a goal in the fewest moves, planning the whole sequence ahead (Tower of London / Hanoi)
problem_solving: goal-state matching under move rules and a move limit, a classic executive planning problem
one_liner: The child moves coloured orbs between pegs to match a goal picture in as few moves as possible, planning the order before touching anything.
interaction: Two rows are shown: the current pegs with stacked orbs and a goal configuration above. The child taps an orb (the top of a peg) to pick it up, then taps a destination peg to drop it (only legal top-moves allowed). A move counter and the goal stay visible. When the current state matches the goal the level completes. Tap-undo reverts the last move. No typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand lifts the top orb from one peg and drops it on another so the pegs match the goal, which flashes to confirm - under 10s. One unscored warm-up needing a single move runs, before scored multi-move goals begin.

learning_science.principle: Planning via the Tower of London paradigm
learning_science.why: Matching a goal configuration in minimum moves is a validated measure of look-ahead planning and executive control.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Goal-match under a move limit with an always-visible target isolates planning; first-move latency and moves-over-minimum are the primary signals.
learning_science.source: Shallice, T. (1982). Specific impairments of planning. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B 298(1089).

learning_science.why: Problem structure (goal hierarchy, move conflicts) drives difficulty, and able planners invest preplanning time to cut wasted moves.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Levels vary goal-subgoal conflict and minimum-move depth, and we score the thinking pause before the first move against later efficiency.
learning_science.source: Kaller, C. P., Rahm, B., Kostering, L., & Unterrainer, J. M. (2011). Reviewing the impact of problem structure on planning. Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews 35(10).

tail_precision_rationale: M-EFF (moves over the minimum) and M-RTFIRST (preplanning latency) are the classic tail separators for planning: strong planners pause, then execute near-optimally, while impulsive solvers move fast and overshoot. M-REV distinguishes committed plans from thrashing and M-PROG traces progress toward the goal state, so a single deep problem yields a graded planning estimate rather than solved/unsolved.
age_rationale: Tap-to-pick and tap-to-drop with large orbs is accessible from 2-3 on two-peg one-move goals. 4-5 uses three pegs and 2-3 move goals; 6-8 uses deep goals with goal-subgoal conflicts and tight move limits that demand several-move look-ahead. No reading and no dragging precision are required.

adaptive.content_range: one-move two-peg goals (2-3) up to deep goal-conflict configurations at the minimum-move limit (6-8 tail)
difficulty_levers: presence of goal-subgoal conflicts (an orb must move away before its final placement)
adaptive.notes: Goal states are generated with a solver storing the minimum-move count for M-EFF and tagging goal-conflict structure; endless parallel forms and above-level depths for ceiling probing.

engagement_hook: Rearranging glowing orbs to match a target and earning fewest-moves stars is a calm, satisfying planning puzzle that rewards thinking ahead.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Large tap targets remove motor demands; the goal is always visible so it measures planning not memory of the target; orbs are pattern/shape coded for colour-vision fairness; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; efficiency not speed is scored so preplanning pauses are rewarded, not penalised.

name: Star Filter
topics_techniques_covered: selective_filtering: the child holds in mind only the target-coloured shapes while ignoring distractors, then reports them after a delay (filter-and-remember)
updating_binding: as new items stream in, the child updates which items belong to which slot/feature, binding item to location
attention_control: sustaining attention on relevant items and suppressing salient distractors over the trial
one_liner: The child watches a brief array, remembers only the target-coloured shapes (ignoring the rest), and after a short blank taps where those shapes were.
interaction: A cue shows the target colour, then several shapes (targets plus distractors) flash briefly and disappear. After a short blank the child taps the grid cells where the target-coloured shapes had been (tap again to deselect), then taps DONE. The number of targets and distractors scales the load. No typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand watches two blue and one grey shape flash, then after the blank taps only the two cells where blue had been, which light green - under 10s, showing you keep only the target colour. One unscored warm-up with one target and one distractor runs before scored higher-load trials begin.

learning_science.principle: Attentional control of access to working memory
learning_science.why: High-capacity individuals differ mainly in excluding irrelevant items from working memory, not in raw storage.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Distractors must be filtered out before the delayed report, so the score reflects filtering efficiency, the individual-difference driver.
learning_science.source: Vogel, E. K., McCollough, A. W., & Machizawa, M. G. (2005). Neural measures reveal individual differences in controlling access to working memory. Nature 438.

learning_science.principle: Executive attention view of working-memory capacity
learning_science.why: Working-memory capacity is largely the ability to control attention and resist interference.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Salient distractors and a retention delay load executive attention, so the task indexes controlled attention rather than passive span.
learning_science.source: Engle, R. W. (2002). Working memory capacity as executive attention. Current Directions in Psychological Science 11(1).

tail_precision_rationale: M-DPRIME separates true filtering sensitivity from guessing (a cautious child and a guesser are not scored alike), and M-FALSEALARM specifically counts distractor intrusions, the purest filtering-failure signal. M-UPDATECOST (accuracy decrement per added distractor) and M-SPAN (staircased target load at criterion) give a continuous capacity estimate that keeps separating high performers who all succeed at low load.
age_rationale: Watch-then-tap-where-it-was is accessible from 2-3 with one target and one distractor and generous timing. 4-5 raises target and distractor counts; 6-8 uses high distractor loads and shorter exposures that separate efficient filterers. Large tap cells and a colour-plus-shape target cue avoid motor and colour-vision confounds; no reading.

adaptive.content_range: one-target one-distractor arrays with long exposure (2-3) up to high-distractor-load brief arrays (6-8 tail)
adaptive.notes: Arrays are procedurally sampled with target load staircased for M-SPAN and distractor count varied for M-UPDATECOST; parallel forms are unlimited and consistency clones support near-cut checks.

engagement_hook: A quick catch-the-stars memory flash with lights and a satisfying reveal keeps children leaning in, and rising loads feel like harder arcade waves.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Targets are cued by colour plus a shape/pattern for colour-vision fairness; large tap cells remove motor demands; timing is tuned per band so processing speed does not contaminate the capacity estimate; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; M-DPRIME corrects for guessing so response bias does not inflate scores.

name: Signal Whack
topics_techniques_covered: response_inhibition_impulse_control: the child taps fast for go targets but must withhold the tap on rare no-go/stop signals (go/no-go and stop-signal)
inhibitory_control_attention: on some rounds flanking distractors point the wrong way and must be ignored while responding to the centre (flanker conflict)
one_liner: The child taps the good critters as fast as they can but must hold still when a stop critter pops up.
interaction: Critters pop up one at a time in holes. Most are green go critters the child taps as fast as possible; a rare red stop critter must NOT be tapped (the child withholds). A later block adds flankers: side critters face the same or the opposite way as the centre and the child taps the centre's direction. Responses and withholds are logged automatically; the round is timed and paced. No typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand taps two green critters quickly, then a red stop critter appears and the hand pulls back and shakes 'no' while the critter ducks away - under 10s, showing tap green, never red. One unscored warm-up with a slow mix of go and stop trials runs before the scored, faster block begins.

learning_science.principle: The horse-race model of response inhibition
learning_science.why: Stopping is a race between a go and a stop process; stop-signal reaction time estimates the latency of the covert inhibitory process.
learning_science.concrete_decision: A staircased stop-signal delay lets us estimate SSRT, one of the least coachable executive metrics, alongside commission errors.
learning_science.source: Logan, G. D., & Cowan, W. B. (1984). On the ability to inhibit thought and action: A theory of an act of control. Psychological Review 91(3).

learning_science.principle: Inhibitory control as a core executive function
learning_science.why: Inhibition (withholding prepotent responses, resisting distractor interference) is a distinct, developmentally central executive function.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The go/no-go plus flanker blocks target prepotent-response inhibition and interference control separately, yielding commission-rate and congruency-cost signals.
learning_science.source: Diamond, A. (2013). Executive functions. Annual Review of Psychology 64.

tail_precision_rationale: M-COMM (no-go commission rate) and M-SSRT (modelled stopping latency) isolate impulse control independent of raw speed, so careful-fast children separate from impulsive-fast ones. M-CONGEFF (incongruent-minus-congruent RT) indexes interference control, and M-POSTERR (post-error slowing) plus M-RTVAR (consistency) add performance-monitoring and worst-performance signals that track ability better than peak speed.
age_rationale: Tap-the-good-one, hold-on-the-bad-one is developmentally appropriate from K-1 (and even 2-3) with slow pacing and large targets; inhibition tasks are validated in early childhood. 4-5 and 6-8 get faster pacing, rarer stop signals and the flanker block for added interference load. All feedback is visual; no reading.

adaptive.content_range: slow go/no-go with obvious stop critters (K-1/2-3) up to fast staircased stop-signal plus incongruent flankers (6-8)
adaptive.notes: Trial streams are generated with parametric no-go probability and a tracking stop-signal delay for SSRT; note inhibition compresses at the very top, so this profiles impulse control and complements high-tail reasoning rather than ranking the extreme tail alone.

engagement_hook: A fast, juicy whack-the-critter arcade with pop animations and a combo meter keeps effort high, while the stop critters add playful surprise.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Large targets and per-band pacing keep it a control task not a motor-speed race; go/no-go stimuli differ by shape not colour alone; anticipatory taps under 150 ms are flagged as false alarms not credited; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; M-COMBO-style accuracy gating ensures speed is credited only with maintained accuracy.

name: Sky Courier
topics_techniques_covered: cognitive_control_speed: the child steers along a path while responding only to specific signs, so single-task and dual-task blocks quantify multitasking cost and speed (NeuroRacer-style)
attention_control: sustaining attention to targets amid distractor signs across a continuous task
selective_filtering: responding to target signs while filtering out non-target signs
response_inhibition_impulse_control: withholding responses to frequent non-target signs
one_liner: The child keeps a flying courier on the path with left/right taps while tapping only when the right delivery sign appears.
interaction: A courier auto-flies down a winding path; the child taps left/right zones to keep it on the path (steering). Delivery signs scroll past; the child taps a COLLECT zone only for target signs and withholds for non-targets. A single-task block (signs only) and a dual-task block (steer plus signs) run so the multitasking cost is measured. All continuous and timed; no typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand taps left/right to nudge the courier back onto the path, then taps COLLECT when the star sign appears and ignores a plain sign - under 10s. One unscored warm-up (slow, signs-only) runs before the scored single-task and dual-task blocks begin.

learning_science.principle: Multitasking cost as a cognitive-control index
learning_science.why: The performance drop from single- to dual-task (multitasking cost), not raw speed, indexes cognitive control and is sensitive across the lifespan.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Matched single- and dual-task blocks let us compute the multitasking cost rather than crediting peak reaction speed.
learning_science.source: Anguera, J. A., et al. (2013). Video game training enhances cognitive control in older adults. Nature 501.

learning_science.why: Intra-individual RT variability and the slowest responses predict ability better than mean or peak speed.
learning_science.concrete_decision: We score RT variability and lapse rate under load, not fastest RT, so consistency of controlled processing drives the estimate.
learning_science.source: Larson, G. E., & Alderton, D. L. (1990). Reaction time variability and intelligence: A worst performance analysis. Intelligence 14(3).

tail_precision_rationale: The dual-minus-single multitasking cost (from M-RT and M-ACC across blocks) is the primary controlled-processing separator, resistant to raw-speed coaching. M-SPEEDACC and M-COMBO credit sustained joint speed-and-accuracy rather than impulsive fast-wrong responding, while M-RTVAR and M-LAPSE apply the worst-performance rule so consistency, not peak speed, drives the tail estimate; M-FALSEALARM guards against crediting impulsive sign-taps.
age_rationale: Simultaneous steering and target-response (a genuine dual task) requires divided attention and enough motor control that it is set from 4-5 (with slow speed and wide paths) up to 6-8 (faster scroll, narrower path, rarer targets). Below 4-5 reliable dual-tasking is developmentally limited, setting the lower bound; no reading is involved.

adaptive.content_range: slow wide-path signs-only steering (4-5) up to fast narrow-path dual-task with rare targets and frequent non-targets (6-8)
adaptive.notes: Courses and sign streams are procedurally generated; single/dual blocks are matched for the multitasking-cost contrast; keep high-load blocks to avoid ceiling on the raw single-task speed.

engagement_hook: A flying-courier arcade with steering and delivery combos is exciting enough to pull maximal effort, so processing speed is measured at true ceiling rather than under boredom.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Wide tap zones and per-band speed keep motor/device latency from dominating; target signs differ by shape not colour alone; the multitasking-cost contrast partials out baseline motor speed; anticipatory taps are flagged; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; M-ENGAGE gates validity on sustained on-task behaviour.

name: Number Quest
topics_techniques_covered: symbolic_magnitude_arithmetic: the child compares and combines quantities across dot, spoken and written-numeral formats to move along a race track (Number Race-style)
place_value_composition: the child composes and regroups target numbers from base-ten blocks (ones/tens/hundreds)
approximate_number_system: the child taps the more numerous of two briefly shown dot herds, with ratio adapting (Panamath-style ANS)
one_liner: The child picks the bigger quantity and builds target numbers from tens-and-ones blocks to race a hero along a number track.
interaction: Three mini-modes advance the hero: (1) two dot herds flash and the child taps the more numerous side; (2) two cards (dots, spoken numeral, or written numeral) appear and the child taps the larger; (3) a target number is shown and the child taps base-ten blocks (ones, tens, hundreds) into a tray to compose it, regrouping ten ones into a ten. Each correct answer moves the hero forward. No typing; numerals are read aloud on tap for pre-readers.
self_teach: The ghost-hand sees two dot herds, taps the fuller side which sparkles and the hero hops forward; then taps one ten-block and three ones to build '13' - under 10s. One unscored warm-up of an easy comparison runs before scored, adaptive items begin.

learning_science.principle: Approximate Number System acuity and math ability
learning_science.why: Non-symbolic number acuity (Weber fraction) relates to symbolic math achievement and is low-literacy and hard to coach.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The dot-comparison mode adapts the ratio to estimate the child's Weber fraction with size/area perceptual controls.
learning_science.source: Halberda, J., Mazzocco, M. M. M., & Feigenson, L. (2008). Individual differences in non-verbal number acuity correlate with maths achievement. Nature 455.

learning_science.why: The precision and linearity of magnitude placement and flexible base-ten composition predict arithmetic competence.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Track movement uses magnitude comparison and the build-a-number mode scores regrouping strategy, targeting place-value understanding not calculation fluency.
learning_science.source: Siegler, R. S., & Opfer, J. E. (2003). The development of numerical estimation: Evidence for multiple representations. Psychological Science 14(3).

tail_precision_rationale: M-WEBER (adaptive dot-ratio acuity) keeps separating strong number sense even where symbolic items would floor in K-1, and M-EFF on the build-a-number mode credits efficient regrouping (one ten plus three ones over thirteen single ones) that marks flexible place-value reasoners. M-ERRTYPE distinguishes a magnitude near-miss from a place-value slip (tens/ones swap), and M-SPEEDACC ensures fast comparisons are credited only when accurate.
age_rationale: Non-symbolic dot comparison and read-aloud numerals let non-readers in K-1 show number sense. 2-3 introduces two-digit place-value building; 4-5 and 6-8 add three-digit regrouping, tighter dot ratios and cross-format (dot vs numeral) comparisons with deadlines. Tap-only input and audio numerals keep literacy and motor load low.

adaptive.content_range: easy dot comparisons and one-ten builds (K-1) up to close-ratio ANS, cross-format magnitude and three-digit regrouping under deadline (6-8 tail)
difficulty_levers: number size and regrouping demand in build mode
adaptive.notes: All three modes are procedurally generated with perceptual controls on dot displays and an auto-checked minimal-block key for M-EFF; the ANS ratio staircases per child for M-WEBER.

engagement_hook: Racing a hero along a track by out-counting and out-building keeps young children motivated, and the always-appropriately-hard adaptive loop sustains effort.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Read-aloud numerals remove reading load; dot displays control for area/density so children count number not blob size; large tap targets and blocks remove motor demands; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; M-SPEEDACC prevents rewarding impulsive fast-wrong comparisons; audio has a captioned/replayable option for accessibility.

name: Word Forge
topics_techniques_covered: orthographic_lexical_access: the child forms as many valid words as possible from given letter tiles under a time budget, indexing lexical access speed and orthographic knowledge (anagram/word-building)
one_liner: The child taps letter tiles to build as many real words as they can before the sand timer runs out.
interaction: A rack of letter tiles is shown. The child taps letters to spell a word into a slot then taps ENTER; valid words score and animate onto a shelf while invalid strings gently shake and clear. Longer and rarer words earn brighter gems. A visible sand timer bounds the round. Tiles can be reused across words. Letters are voiced on tap to support emerging readers. No keyboard typing (tap-to-build only).
self_teach: The ghost-hand taps C-A-T then ENTER; the word flies onto the shelf with a chime, then taps C-A-T-S for a bigger gem - under 10s, showing build words, longer is better. One unscored warm-up round on an easy rack runs before the scored, timed round begins.

learning_science.why: Fluent readers rapidly connect letter strings to known words; speed and breadth of this access is a strong verbal-ability marker.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Scoring rewards number, length and rarity of valid words produced under time, indexing orthographic-lexical access rather than handwriting or spelling dictation.
learning_science.source: Ehri, L. C. (2005). Learning to read words: Theory, findings, and issues. Scientific Studies of Reading 9(2).

learning_science.principle: Productive fluency as an ability signal
learning_science.why: Open production (generate many valid items) lowers the ceiling and reveals verbal breadth beyond recognition items.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The child produces words freely rather than selecting from options, so fluency and lexical depth separate the tail; letter audio lowers the decoding barrier.
learning_science.source: Carroll, J. B. (1993). Human Cognitive Abilities: A Survey of Factor-Analytic Studies. Cambridge University Press.

tail_precision_rationale: M-IDEAFLU (count of distinct valid words) and M-VOCABLVL (rarest word-frequency band produced) are ceiling-resistant fluency and lexical-depth signals that keep separating strong verbal children after common short words are exhausted. M-RTFIRST (time to first valid word) and inter-word latency index lexical-access speed, while M-FLEX (variety of word length/root families) distinguishes deep lexicons from repetitive stems.
age_rationale: Building short words from tiles with letter audio is accessible once basic letter-sound knowledge emerges (2-3), with easy high-frequency racks. 4-5 adds longer racks and length bonuses; 6-8 uses racks that afford rare/long words and tighter timers that reward deep lexical access. Tap-to-build avoids handwriting/keyboard demands. Below 2-3 letter knowledge is generally insufficient, setting the floor.

adaptive.content_range: short high-frequency word racks (2-3) up to racks affording long/rare words under tight time (6-8 tail)
difficulty_levers: letter set (how many long/rare words it affords)
adaptive.notes: Racks are generated against a frequency-tagged lexicon that guarantees a known set of valid words for scoring M-IDEAFLU and M-VOCABLVL; unlimited parallel racks matched on solution count.

engagement_hook: Forging words into glowing gems against a sand timer is a satisfying race, and chasing longer/rarer words for bigger gems drives effortful production.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Letters are voiced on tap so decoding does not block emerging readers; tap-to-build removes handwriting/keyboard motor load; the validated lexicon avoids penalising legitimate rare words; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; scoring weights breadth and rarity over raw speed so thoughtful producers are not penalised.

name: Story Detective
topics_techniques_covered: listening_comprehension_inference: an audio/animated story pauses for comprehension and inference probes (who wanted what, why, what happens next), scored on inference depth without a reading-decoding barrier
one_liner: The child listens to a short animated story and taps picture answers to who-wanted-what and why-and-what-next questions.
interaction: A narrated, animated scene plays (audio plus simple animation). At set points it pauses and shows 3-4 picture options for a spoken question probing literal recall, a bridging inference, a causal why, or a prediction. The child taps the best picture; a REPLAY button re-plays the last narration segment. Answers and re-listens are logged. No reading required; all prompts are spoken with picture options.
self_teach: The ghost-hand listens as a puppy hides a bone, then a spoken question shows three pictures and the hand taps the bone-under-tree picture, which glows - under 10s, showing listen then tap the picture that answers. One unscored warm-up (a literal who-question) runs before scored, deeper-inference probes begin.

learning_science.why: Comprehension builds a situation model by integrating text with inference; deeper inference marks stronger comprehenders.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Probes are tagged by inference depth (literal, bridging, causal, predictive) so the deepest level reached is measured, targeting integration not recall.
learning_science.source: Kintsch, W. (1988). The role of knowledge in discourse comprehension: A construction-integration model. Psychological Review 95(2).

learning_science.principle: Listening comprehension in the Simple View of Reading
learning_science.why: Language comprehension is separable from decoding; assessing it by ear reveals verbal talent independent of reading fluency.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Delivery is fully audio with picture responses so the score isolates language comprehension and inference from decoding ability.
learning_science.source: Gough, P. B., & Tunmer, W. E. (1986). Decoding, reading, and reading disability. Remedial and Special Education 7(1).

tail_precision_rationale: M-INFDEPTH (deepest inference layer answered correctly: literal to bridging to causal to predictive/evaluative) is the sharpest tail separator because comprehension discrimination at the top is about inference layer, not literal recall. M-LURETYPE reads which distractor class (literal-but-irrelevant, plausible-but-uncaused, thematic associate) pulls errors, refining placement, and M-HINT (re-listens used) adds a dynamic-assessment learning-rate signal.
age_rationale: Audio delivery with picture answers makes deep comprehension accessible to non-readers from K-1. Difficulty scales by story length, syntactic complexity and inference depth: K-1/2-3 short stories with literal and simple bridging probes, 4-5 and 6-8 longer narratives with causal, predictive and evaluative inference. No reading at any band.

adaptive.content_range: short stories with literal/bridging probes (K-1) up to longer narratives with causal, predictive and evaluative inference (6-8 tail)
adaptive.notes: Story skeletons are templated with slot-filled characters/goals and depth-tagged probe banks with designed lures; new narrations require audio generation, so cloning is moderate rather than fully automatic.

engagement_hook: Being a detective inside an animated story and solving what-happens-next keeps children listening intently, with replays framed as re-watching clues.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Full audio plus picture options removes reading/decoding load; replays are logged (as hint use) so re-listens are measured not blocked; distractors are designed by lure type not trickery; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; narration uses controlled vocabulary and offers captions so hearing-access needs are supported.

name: Claim Duel
topics_techniques_covered: verbal_reasoning_argumentation: the child builds a position by matching the strongest evidence to a claim and rebuts opposing arguments, scored on claim-evidence link quality (Argubot-style argumentation)
one_liner: The child props up a claim by dragging the strongest evidence cards to it and knocks down a rival claim by picking its weakest link.
interaction: A claim card is shown with a pool of evidence cards (some strongly relevant, some weakly/irrelevantly related, some off-topic). The child taps evidence cards to attach them to the claim, building the strongest support; then in a duel a rival claim appears and the child taps the evidence that best rebuts it. Strength meters fill by link quality. Picture/icon-supported cards with short audio labels keep reading load low. No typing.
self_teach: The ghost-hand taps the on-topic strong-evidence card onto the claim (its strength bar fills green) and skips the off-topic card (which greys out) - under 10s, showing attach strong evidence, not weak. One unscored warm-up with one clearly strong and one clearly irrelevant card runs before scored, subtler items begin.

learning_science.why: Strong arguments link claims to data via warrants; recognising and building those links is the core of argumentation skill.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Cards are typed as claim, evidence (strong/weak) and warrant so the child's attachments are scored against argument structure, not surface agreement.
learning_science.source: Toulmin, S. E. (1958). The Uses of Argument. Cambridge University Press.

learning_science.principle: Argument skill as coordinating claims and counterclaims
learning_science.why: Mature reasoning evaluates evidence and integrates counterarguments rather than only supporting one's own view.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The rebuttal phase requires attacking the rival claim's weakest evidence, measuring evaluation of counterclaims not just one-sided support.
learning_science.source: Kuhn, D. (1991). The Skills of Argument. Cambridge University Press.

tail_precision_rationale: M-POLY (graded claim-evidence link quality) extracts multiple bits of tail information from one rich item, and M-LURETYPE reveals whether errors are pulled by thematic-associate or weak-but-related lures, grading discrimination of evidential relevance. M-PATH preserves the attach/rebut sequence for evidence-model scoring of argument construction, while M-RTFIRST and M-REV separate deliberate evidence evaluation from surface matching.
age_rationale: Coordinating claims with supporting versus irrelevant evidence, and evaluating a counter-claim, requires emerging metacognitive argument skills generally accessible from 4-5 with concrete, picture-supported topics, extending to 6-8 with abstract claims, subtler lures and multi-card warrants. Below 4-5 explicit claim-evidence coordination is developmentally limited, setting the floor; audio labels keep reading load low.

adaptive.content_range: one-strong-one-irrelevant concrete claims (4-5) up to abstract claims with subtle weak-but-related lures and multi-step warrants (6-8 tail)
difficulty_levers: evidence-relevance subtlety (strong vs weak vs thematic lure)
requirement to supply a warrant linking data to claim
adaptive.notes: Claim/evidence sets are templated with relevance-tagged cards and lure classes for M-LURETYPE; strong topical variety needs curation, so cloning is moderate.

engagement_hook: A friendly debate duel where strong evidence powers up your side and rebuttals knock down the rival makes reasoning feel like a battle, driving effortful evaluation.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Picture-plus-audio cards keep reading load low; tap-to-attach removes typing; cards are typed by evidential role so scoring reflects link quality not opinion agreement; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; topics are kept culturally neutral and non-controversial so background knowledge does not confound the reasoning score.

name: Robot Feelings
topics_techniques_covered: empathy_emotion_recognition: as a robot on a social quest the child identifies facial emotions and gauges their intensity to help characters, scoring empathic accuracy and calibration (Crystals-of-Kaydor-style)
one_liner: The child helps a friendly robot by reading each character's face - naming the feeling and how strong it is - to choose the kind response.
interaction: An expressive character face is shown in a short social scene. The child taps the matching emotion (from picture-emotion buttons: happy, sad, angry, scared, surprised, calm) then sets an intensity slider (a little to a lot). The scene then offers 2-3 response actions and the child taps the most helpful one. Empathic accuracy, intensity calibration and response choice are logged. Emotion buttons are icon-based with audio labels; no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand looks at a crying face, taps the sad button, slides intensity high, then taps the offer-a-tissue response which makes the character smile - under 10s, showing read the face, then help. One unscored warm-up on a clearly happy face runs before scored, subtler blended-emotion items begin.

learning_science.principle: Facial emotion recognition as a social-cognition building block
learning_science.why: Reading emotions from faces is a foundational, measurable component of empathy and social intelligence.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Items use validated basic-emotion expressions with graded intensity so accuracy and fine intensity discrimination are both scored.
learning_science.source: Ekman, P. (1992). An argument for basic emotions. Cognition and Emotion 6(3-4).

learning_science.why: Beyond labelling, judging emotion intensity and choosing apt responses indexes empathic accuracy and calibration.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The intensity slider and response choice yield calibration (how well confidence/intensity matches the true state), adding signal beyond the label.
learning_science.source: Ickes, W. (1993). Empathic accuracy. Journal of Personality 61(4).

tail_precision_rationale: M-POLY (graded intensity-calibration score) turns each face into a fine-grained signal that avoids the ceiling of basic-emotion labelling, and M-CONF captures calibration between chosen intensity and the true expression. M-ERRTYPE reads which confusable emotion (fear-vs-surprise, anger-vs-sadness) is mistaken, so subtle blends at high difficulty separate highly empathic children from those who only read prototypical expressions.
age_rationale: Recognising prototypical happy/sad/angry faces is accessible from 2-3 with icon buttons and audio labels. 4-5 adds fear/surprise and coarse intensity; 6-8 adds blended/subtle expressions, fine intensity calibration and context-appropriate response selection that separate advanced social reasoners. All input is tap/slide with audio, so no reading is needed.

adaptive.content_range: prototypical single-emotion faces (2-3) up to subtle blended expressions with fine intensity and context-dependent responses (6-8 tail)
adaptive.notes: Faces are parameterised expression sets with graded intensity for M-POLY; subtle blends and diverse faces need curation, so cloning is moderate; include diverse faces to avoid own-group bias and subtle blends to avoid ceiling.

engagement_hook: Helping a lovable robot make friends by reading feelings is a warm narrative hook that elicits authentic empathic behaviour rather than test-like responding.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Icon buttons plus audio labels remove reading load; tap/slide input removes motor precision demands; use a demographically diverse, validated face set to avoid own-race/own-age recognition bias; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; scoring credits calibrated intensity over a single label so lucky prototypical hits do not inflate the estimate; keep scenarios culturally neutral.

name: Aqueduct Lab
topics_techniques_covered: systems_causal_reasoning: the child lays and rotates pipes, valves and pumps so opening the tap causes water to flow through the whole network and fill a far tank
systems_reasoning: connected pipes behave as one coupled flow system, so a change to one segment propagates through the network
mechanical_systems_reasoning: valves, pumps and water-wheels transmit and gate flow; the child predicts and exploits those mechanical effects
problem_solving: an open constraint-satisfaction goal (route water to the tank within a piece budget) solved by planning, building, testing and revising
one_liner: The child lays and rotates pipes, valves and pumps so water flows from the tap through the network and fills the far tank.
interaction: A tap on the left, an empty goal tank on the right and some fixed rocks sit on a grid, with a tray of pipe pieces (straight, elbow, T-split), a valve and a pump below. The child taps a piece then taps an empty cell to place it, taps a placed piece to rotate or remove it, opens or closes valves by tapping them, then taps FLOW to run the water and watch it travel. If the tank does not fill they adjust pieces and run again. No typing, no reading.
self_teach: A wordless ghost-hand drops two straight pipes and one elbow to connect the tap to the tank, taps FLOW, and blue water runs across and fills the tank which sparkles - under 10s. One unscored warm-up (one straight gap to bridge) gives a happy fill or a gentle reset before scored levels begin.

learning_science.why: Routing a continuous medium requires reasoning about how connected parts pass flow together as one system, echoing validated physics-sandbox assessment.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Levels are built around connectivity and flow direction so success depends on causal system reasoning rather than luck.
learning_science.source: Shute, V. J., Ventura, M., & Kim, Y. J. (2013). Assessment and learning of qualitative physics in Newton's Playground. Journal of Educational Research 106(6).

learning_science.why: Process telemetry from an open build separates how a child reasons from whether the tank finally fills.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Every placement, rotation, valve toggle and run is logged and scored against a systems-reasoning evidence model, not only the final fill.
learning_science.source: Shute, V. J. (2011). Stealth assessment in computer-based games to support learning. In Tobias & Fletcher (Eds.), Computer Games and Instruction.

tail_precision_rationale: M-EFF (pipes and reruns versus the minimal network) and M-HYP (whether each rerun is a disambiguating test of the blockage versus random re-piping) separate strong causal-system reasoners from trial-and-error plumbers even when both eventually fill the tank. M-RTFIRST captures the reflective planning pause before the first placement, M-PATH and M-EXPLORE preserve the full build for evidence-model scoring, and M-PERSIST on hard levels adds tail task-commitment.
age_rationale: Tap-to-place with large snap cells removes fine-motor demands so children from 2-3 can build single-gap runs. 2-3 gets one straight connection; 4-5 adds elbows and one valve; 6-8 adds pumps, T-splits feeding two tanks and tight piece budgets that require multi-step flow foresight. Pre-literacy is fine because all instruction is the wordless ghost-hand.

adaptive.content_range: one-straight-pipe gaps (2-3) up to multi-branch networks with pumps, splits and strict budgets (6-8 tail)
difficulty_levers: network length and number of turns
presence of leaks or blocked cells
adaptive.notes: Grids and tap layouts are procedurally sampled and a solver verifies solvability and the minimal piece count for M-EFF, giving unlimited parallel forms.

engagement_hook: Watching water rush through pipes you connected and burst into the tank is instantly satisfying, and tighter budgets feel like harder plumbing puzzles.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Tap-to-place snapping removes precision-drag motor load; pieces differ by shape and icon not colour alone; flow is deterministic so outcomes reflect reasoning not chaos; ghost-hand plus warm-up neutralises game-novelty variance; efficiency not speed is scored so reflective builders are not penalised.

name: Pulley Hoist
topics_techniques_covered: mechanical_systems_reasoning: the child arranges pulleys, ropes, levers and counterweights so pulling the handle lifts a heavy crate, exploiting mechanical advantage
systems_causal_reasoning: pulling the handle causes a chain of rope and lever motions; the child predicts the causal outcome at the crate
systems_reasoning: the rig is one coupled system where adding a pulley or weight changes the whole lift
problem_solving: reach the lift goal with a limited set of parts, a constraint-satisfaction design task
one_liner: The child arranges pulleys, ropes, levers and counterweights so pulling the handle lifts the heavy crate onto the high platform.
interaction: A crate sits on the ground and a target platform is up high; a frame has peg points where the child mounts pulleys and levers from a tray, runs a rope over mounted pulleys by tapping them in order, and hangs counterweights. The child then taps PULL to run the rig and see whether the crate rises to the platform. Tap a mounted part to rotate or remove it. No typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand mounts one pulley, runs the rope over it to the crate, hangs a weight, taps PULL, and the crate rises onto the platform with a clink - under 10s, showing pulleys and weights lift loads. One unscored warm-up (lift a light crate one step) runs before scored heavier lifts begin.

learning_science.why: People reason about pulleys and levers by mentally animating components, and expertise shows as chunked rule use (mechanical advantage, direction of pull).
learning_science.concrete_decision: The rig animates on PULL so children can run and inspect their mental model, and difficulty rises with mechanical-advantage demands that reward rule-based reasoning.
learning_science.source: Hegarty, M. (1992). Mental animation: Inferring motion from static displays of mechanical systems. Journal of Experimental Psychology: LMC 18(5).

learning_science.why: An open build lets us score how the child assembles a working machine rather than only whether the crate rises.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Each mount, rope routing, weight and rerun is logged against a mechanical-reasoning evidence model.
learning_science.source: Mislevy, R. J., Almond, R. G., & Lukas, J. F. (2003). A brief introduction to evidence-centered design. ETS Research Report RR-03-16.

tail_precision_rationale: M-EFF (parts and pulls versus the minimal rig) and M-ERRTYPE (a too-few-pulleys under-lift versus a wrong rope path versus insufficient counterweight) resolve near-misses into the specific mechanical principle a child has or lacks. M-HYP indexes whether reruns are disambiguating tests of mechanical advantage, and M-RTFIRST credits the planning pause before the first mount that marks strong mechanical reasoners.
age_rationale: Tap-to-mount with large snap pegs removes fine-motor load so 2-3 can lift a light crate with one pulley. 4-5 adds a lever and one counterweight; 6-8 adds multi-pulley blocks, mechanical-advantage targets and strict part budgets that demand multiplicative mechanical reasoning. All instruction is the wordless ghost-hand.

adaptive.content_range: one-pulley light lifts (2-3) up to multi-pulley mechanical-advantage rigs with counterweights and budgets (6-8 tail)
difficulty_levers: number of pulleys and levers needed
adaptive.notes: Rigs are procedurally sampled and a physics solver stores the minimal working configuration for M-EFF and M-ACC, giving unlimited parallel forms.

engagement_hook: Rigging ropes and pulleys and watching a too-heavy crate finally rise gives a real engineering thrill, and heavier crates feel like tougher levels.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Snap-to-peg mounting removes precision-drag load; parts differ by silhouette not colour; the animation makes the lift outcome unambiguous; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; crediting efficient minimal rigs over rapid part-spamming avoids rewarding fast guessing.

name: Path Coder
topics_techniques_covered: spatial_navigation: the child plans a whole route and programs a robot to walk it through a grid world to collect keys and reach the door
planning_lookahead: the full action sequence is committed before any feedback, forcing forward planning
problem_solving: find an efficient command sequence satisfying collect-keys-then-exit under a step budget
one_liner: The child lines up a sequence of move and turn arrows, then taps RUN so the robot walks the whole planned route to collect keys and reach the door.
interaction: A top-down grid shows a robot, keys, walls and a door. Below is a program strip; the child taps arrow tiles (forward, turn-left, turn-right) to append steps to the strip, taps a step to delete it, then taps RUN to execute the entire sequence at once and watch the robot move. If the robot hits a wall or misses a key they edit the program and run again. No typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand taps forward, forward, turn, forward into the strip, taps RUN, and the robot walks to the key then the door which opens - under 10s, showing build the plan then run it. One unscored warm-up (two forward steps to the door) runs before scored routes begin.

learning_science.principle: Planning measured by look-ahead before acting
learning_science.why: Committing to a whole action sequence before any feedback forces genuine forward planning rather than reactive step-by-step correction.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The child must queue and run a full program, so first-run success and edits-to-solve index planning quality.
learning_science.source: Shallice, T. (1982). Specific impairments of planning. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B 298(1089).

learning_science.why: Sequencing turns relative to the robot's own heading requires building and transforming a spatial representation of the route.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Turn tiles are relative to the robot's facing so success reflects mental route simulation not trial taps.
learning_science.source: Tolman, E. C. (1948). Cognitive maps in rats and men. Psychological Review 55(4).

tail_precision_rationale: M-EFF (program length and reruns versus the optimal sequence) is a continuous ceiling-resistant separator; first-run success and M-REV (edits before a correct run) distinguish children who mentally simulate the route from those who patch by trial. M-RTFIRST captures the planning time before the first tile and M-PROG traces keys collected across runs.
age_rationale: Tapping a few big arrow tiles then RUN is accessible from 2-3 on tiny two-step routes with no turns. 4-5 adds relative turns and one key; 6-8 uses long routes with multiple keys, forced ordering and step budgets that demand several-step look-ahead. No reading and no drag precision are needed.

adaptive.content_range: two-step no-turn routes (2-3) up to long multi-key routes with relative turns and tight step budgets (6-8 tail)
adaptive.notes: Grids are procedurally generated with a solver storing the optimal program length for M-EFF and unlimited parallel forms.

engagement_hook: Programming a robot and watching it march out your whole plan at once is a beloved coding-toy mechanic, with fewest-steps stars rewarding elegant routes.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Large arrow tiles remove motor demands; the whole grid is visible so it taxes planning not memory; walls and keys are high-contrast and shape-coded; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; efficiency not speed is scored so planners who pause are rewarded.

name: Path Forge
topics_techniques_covered: manipulation: the child rotates and places road tiles, mentally and physically transforming pieces to line up a connected route
spatial_navigation: the assembled road defines a route from the start hut to the goal that a courier then walks
planning_lookahead: connecting the road without wasted tiles requires ordering placements several steps ahead
problem_solving: build one continuous coin-collecting path under a tile budget, a spatial constraint-satisfaction goal
one_liner: The child rotates and drops road tiles to build one continuous path from the start hut to the goal, then the courier walks the route.
interaction: A grid shows a start hut, a goal flag and some blocked cells, with a tray of road tiles (straight, curve, T). The child taps a tile then taps an empty cell to place it, taps a placed tile to rotate it or remove it, building a connected road; then taps GO and the courier walks whatever continuous path exists from start to goal, collecting coins on the way. No typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand drops a straight tile and a curve tile to join the hut to the flag, rotates the curve to line up, taps GO, and the courier strolls to the flag - under 10s, showing rotate and place tiles to make a road. One unscored warm-up (one straight tile bridges the gap) runs before scored layouts begin.

learning_science.principle: Spatial ability is malleable and manipulation is a core factor
learning_science.why: Rotating and placing tiles to satisfy connectivity exercises the object-manipulation spatial factor distinct from static pattern recognition.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Correct orientation of each tile is required to connect the road, so the task targets mental rotation plus placement.
learning_science.source: Uttal, D. H., et al. (2013). The malleability of spatial skills: A meta-analysis of training studies. Psychological Bulletin 139(2).

learning_science.why: Choosing the shortest connected route that visits coins is a spatial route-optimisation problem.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Tiles used and route length versus the optimal are scored so planful routing beats haphazard tiling.
learning_science.source: Shallice, T. (1982). Specific impairments of planning. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B 298(1089).

tail_precision_rationale: M-EFF (tiles and rotations versus the minimal connecting path) resists ceiling on dense boards; M-REV (re-rotations and re-placements) separates children who mentally pre-rotate each tile from guess-and-turn solvers. M-RTFIRST captures the planning pause and M-PROG turns one board into a coins-collected trajectory.
age_rationale: Tap-place-then-tap-rotate with large tiles is accessible from 2-3 on one-tile gaps. 4-5 adds curves and multiple tiles; 6-8 uses large boards with obstacles, required coin pickups and tile budgets that demand rotation foresight and route optimisation. No reading or drag precision needed.

adaptive.content_range: one-straight-tile gaps (2-3) up to large obstacle boards with curves, coins and tile budgets (6-8 tail)
adaptive.notes: Boards are procedurally generated with a solver storing the minimal connecting-path tile count for M-EFF and unlimited parallel forms.

engagement_hook: Snapping and spinning road tiles to forge a path and then watching the little courier stroll it is a cosy building hook, with fewest-tiles stars for tidy routes.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Tap-then-rotate placement removes precise-drag load; tiles are shape and pattern distinct; the full board is visible so it taxes manipulation and planning not memory; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; tile efficiency not speed is scored.

name: Shape Smith
topics_techniques_covered: manipulation: the child rotates and flips puzzle pieces and places them to exactly fill a target silhouette
planning_lookahead: fitting the last piece requires ordering which piece goes where several steps ahead
problem_solving: a spatial constraint-satisfaction goal (fill the outline with no gaps or overlaps) under a move budget
spatial_visualization_construction: mentally previewing how a reoriented piece will occupy the space before placing it
one_liner: The child rotates and flips a few puzzle pieces and drops them so they exactly fill the target silhouette with no gaps or overlaps.
interaction: A blank target outline sits in the middle with a tray of tangram-like pieces below. The child taps a piece to select it, taps rotate or flip buttons to orient it, then taps a spot inside the outline to place it (tap a placed piece to pick it up again). When every piece fits and the outline is fully covered the shape lights up. A move and rotation counter shows effort. No typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand takes a triangle, taps rotate twice, drops it into a corner of the outline, then slots a square beside it and the outline glows full - under 10s, showing turn pieces to make them fit. One unscored warm-up (two pieces into an easy outline) runs before scored silhouettes begin.

learning_science.principle: Spatial manipulation as a trainable STEM-predictive factor
learning_science.why: Mentally rotating and flipping pieces to fit a frame is the core object-transformation spatial factor.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Pieces must be reoriented before they fit, so the task isolates manipulation rather than recognition.
learning_science.source: Uttal, D. H., et al. (2013). The malleability of spatial skills: A meta-analysis of training studies. Psychological Bulletin 139(2).

learning_science.why: Fitting the last piece requires setting sub-goals about which piece goes where first, a hallmark of planful problem solving.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Pieces-over-minimum and rotation efficiency are scored so decomposing the fill is credited over blind dropping.
learning_science.source: Newell, A., & Simon, H. A. (1972). Human Problem Solving. Prentice-Hall.

tail_precision_rationale: M-EFF (rotations and placements versus the minimal solution) is a fine continuous discriminator on hard silhouettes; M-REV separates confident pre-visualised placements from rotate-and-try. M-RTFIRST captures the pre-placement visualisation pause and M-PROG turns one hard fill into a coverage trajectory beyond solved/unsolved.
age_rationale: Tap-rotate-then-place with large pieces and snapping is accessible from 2-3 on two-piece outlines. 4-5 adds flips and three-to-four pieces; 6-8 uses many-piece silhouettes with mirror-sensitive fits and rotation budgets that demand mental transformation. No reading or precise dragging.

adaptive.content_range: two-piece easy outlines (2-3) up to many-piece mirror-sensitive silhouettes (6-8 tail)
difficulty_levers: need for flips versus rotations only
adaptive.notes: Silhouettes are generated from piece sets with a solver storing the minimal orientation moves for M-EFF and unlimited parallel forms.

engagement_hook: The click of a rotated piece snapping perfectly into a silhouette is deeply satisfying, and fewest-turns stars reward elegant fits.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Tap-rotate-then-place removes precise drag and rotate motor load; pieces are shape distinct; the outline is fully visible so it taxes manipulation not memory; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; move efficiency not speed is scored.

name: Burrow Echo
topics_techniques_covered: updating_binding: the child continuously updates and rebinds the remembered target as critters stream from burrows, tapping when the current one matches the one n steps back (n-back)
attention_control: sustaining attention across a paced stream while maintaining the rolling comparison
selective_filtering: rejecting near-lure critters (the n-back-but-one) that must be filtered from the true match
one_liner: The child watches critters pop from burrows one at a time and taps MATCH whenever the current critter is the same as the one that popped a set number of steps back.
interaction: Critters appear one at a time in a row of burrows. The child taps a big MATCH button when the current critter matches the one from n pops earlier (n starts at 1 and rises); otherwise they wait for the next. Occasional near-lures (the n-back-but-one critter) test filtering. Hits, misses and false alarms are logged automatically; the stream is paced. No typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand watches a fox, then a bird, then a fox again and taps MATCH as the second fox appears while the burrow glows green - under 10s, showing tap when it is the same as before. One unscored warm-up at 1-back with slow pacing runs before the scored, faster and higher-n stream begins.

learning_science.principle: Working-memory updating via the n-back paradigm
learning_science.why: Continuously replacing the remembered target as the stream advances is a pure updating-and-binding operation linked to fluid intelligence.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The child binds each critter to its recent position and updates the comparison target every pop, isolating updating.
learning_science.source: Jaeggi, S. M., Buschkuehl, M., Perrig, W. J., & Meier, B. (2010). The concurrent validity of the N-back task as a working memory measure. Memory 18(4).

learning_science.principle: Attentional control of access to working memory
learning_science.why: Rejecting near-lures requires excluding highly similar but wrong items from the comparison, the individual-difference driver of capacity.
learning_science.concrete_decision: N-back-but-one lures load filtering so d-prime reflects controlled attention not raw storage.
learning_science.source: Engle, R. W. (2002). Working memory capacity as executive attention. Current Directions in Psychological Science 11(1).

tail_precision_rationale: M-DPRIME separates true match sensitivity from guessing and M-FALSEALARM counts lure intrusions (the purest filtering failure). M-UPDATECOST (accuracy decrement per added level of n) and M-SPAN (highest n sustained at criterion) give a continuous updating-capacity estimate that keeps separating high performers who all succeed at 1-back.
age_rationale: Watch-then-tap-MATCH at 1-back with slow pacing is accessible from 2-3 (child n-back is validated in early childhood). 4-5 raises pace and adds lures; 6-8 runs 2-3-back at speed with frequent lures that separate efficient updaters. Large tap target and no reading keep motor and literacy load low.

adaptive.content_range: slow 1-back with few lures (2-3) up to fast 2-3-back with frequent near-lures (6-8 tail)
adaptive.notes: Streams are procedurally generated with n staircased for M-SPAN and lure rate varied for M-FALSEALARM and M-DPRIME.

engagement_hook: A quick whack-of-recognition rhythm with pop animations and a match streak keeps children leaning in, and rising n feels like harder arcade waves.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Critters differ by shape not colour alone; a large MATCH target removes motor demands; pacing is tuned per band so speed does not contaminate the capacity estimate; anticipatory taps under 150 ms are flagged; M-DPRIME corrects for guessing; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty.

name: Firefly Jars
topics_techniques_covered: updating_binding: the child binds each firefly to its jar and updates that binding as the jars slide and swap positions (multiple-object tracking)
selective_filtering: distractor bugs buzz in and must be filtered from the target fireflies
attention_control: sustaining divided attention across several moving targets over the trial
