one_liner: The child watches which jars catch the glowing fireflies, keeps tracking them as the jars slide and swap places, then taps the jars that still hold a firefly.
interaction: A few fireflies fly into some jars (which briefly glow) while other jars stay empty; lids close and the jars then slide around and swap positions several times. Ordinary bugs also buzz in as distractors and must be ignored. When motion stops the child taps every jar they believe holds a firefly (tap again to deselect) then taps DONE; correct jars sparkle. Number of fireflies, swaps and distractors scales the load. No typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand watches one jar glow with a firefly, follows it as two jars swap, then taps the jar in its new spot which sparkles - under 10s, showing keep your eye on the firefly jar as they move. One unscored warm-up (one firefly, one swap) runs before scored higher-load rounds begin.

learning_science.why: Following target jars through motion requires continuously updating a bound representation of which object is where, taxing spatial updating and binding.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Jars swap positions so the child must update bindings rather than memorise fixed locations.
learning_science.source: Pylyshyn, Z. W., & Storm, R. W. (1988). Tracking multiple independent targets: Evidence for a parallel tracking mechanism. Spatial Vision 3(3).

learning_science.why: Ignoring buzzing distractor bugs while holding targets loads controlled attention, the driver of capacity differences.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Salient distractors must be filtered so the score reflects filtering and sustained attention not passive span.
learning_science.source: Engle, R. W. (2002). Working memory capacity as executive attention. Current Directions in Psychological Science 11(1).

tail_precision_rationale: M-DPRIME distinguishes true tracking sensitivity from guessing and M-FALSEALARM counts distractor-jar taps (filtering failures). M-UPDATECOST (accuracy decrement per added swap or firefly) and M-SPAN (max fireflies tracked at criterion) give a continuous updating-capacity estimate that keeps separating high performers.
age_rationale: Watching one firefly through a single slow swap and tapping its jar is accessible from 2-3. 4-5 adds more fireflies and swaps; 6-8 uses many targets, many fast swaps and salient distractors that separate efficient trackers. Large jar tap targets and no reading keep motor and literacy load low.

adaptive.content_range: one firefly, one slow swap (2-3) up to many fireflies with many fast swaps and distractors (6-8 tail)
adaptive.notes: Rounds are procedurally generated with firefly count staircased for M-SPAN and swaps and distractors varied for M-UPDATECOST and M-FALSEALARM.

engagement_hook: Keeping your eye on glowing fireflies as jars shuffle is a playful shell-game that pulls focused attention, and more swaps feel like a faster magic trick.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Fireflies versus bugs differ by shape and animation not colour alone; large jar targets remove motor demands; swap speed is tuned per band so processing speed does not contaminate capacity; M-DPRIME corrects for guessing; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty.

name: Arrow Storm
topics_techniques_covered: inhibitory_control_attention: on flanker and Simon trials the child responds to the central arrow's direction while suppressing conflicting flankers or position (interference control)
response_inhibition_impulse_control: on rare no-go trials the child must withhold the tap entirely
cognitive_control_speed: resolving conflict quickly under a response deadline indexes controlled-processing speed
attention_control: sustaining focus on the relevant arrow across a fast paced block
one_liner: The child taps the way the middle arrow points as fast as they can, ignoring the arrows beside it, and must not tap at all when a red X flashes.
interaction: A row of five arrows appears; the child taps a big LEFT or RIGHT zone matching the direction of the centre arrow while the flanking arrows point the same (congruent) or opposite (incongruent) way. On some Simon trials a single arrow appears on the left or right side and the child must respond to its direction not its position. On rare no-go trials a red X appears and the child must withhold. Responses, conflicts and withholds are logged; the block is speeded. No typing, no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand sees an arrow row pointing right (sides point left), taps RIGHT and it flashes green, then a red X appears and the hand pulls back - under 10s, showing follow the middle arrow, never tap on the X. One unscored warm-up of slow congruent trials runs before the fast conflict block begins.

learning_science.principle: Inhibition as interference plus prepotent-response control
learning_science.why: Flanker and Simon conflict tax interference control while no-go trials tax prepotent-response inhibition, two distinct facets of executive inhibition.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Mixing flanker, Simon and no-go trials yields separate congruency-cost and commission signals in one speeded task.
learning_science.source: Diamond, A. (2013). Executive functions. Annual Review of Psychology 64.

learning_science.why: Intra-individual RT variability and the slowest responses predict ability better than peak speed.
learning_science.concrete_decision: RT variability and accuracy-gated speed are scored rather than fastest RT, so consistency of controlled processing drives the estimate.
learning_science.source: Larson, G. E., & Alderton, D. L. (1990). Reaction time variability and intelligence: A worst performance analysis. Intelligence 14(3).

tail_precision_rationale: M-CONGEFF (incongruent-minus-congruent RT) isolates interference control independent of baseline speed and M-COMM (no-go commission) isolates impulse control, so careful-fast children separate from impulsive-fast ones. M-RTVAR and M-POSTERR add worst-performance and performance-monitoring signals while M-COMBO credits sustained speed only when accuracy holds.
age_rationale: Tap-the-way-it-points with big side zones is developmentally appropriate from K-1 (child flanker is validated in early childhood) with slow pacing and few incongruent trials. 2-3 and 4-5 add Simon and rare no-go trials; 6-8 gets fast pacing, more conflict and rarer no-go that separate efficient controllers. All feedback is visual; no reading.

adaptive.content_range: slow mostly-congruent trials (K-1) up to fast high-conflict flanker plus Simon with rare no-go (6-8)
adaptive.notes: Trial streams are procedurally generated with parametric congruency and no-go rates; inhibition compresses at the very top so this profiles control and complements high-tail reasoning.

engagement_hook: A fast arrow-reflex game with a green-flash combo and surprise red-X freezes keeps effort high while measuring control at true speed.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Large side zones and per-band pacing keep it a control task not a motor-speed race; arrows differ by orientation not colour; anticipatory taps under 150 ms are flagged not credited; M-COMBO gates speed on accuracy; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty.

name: Rule Rush
topics_techniques_covered: cognitive_control_speed: the child switches the active sorting rule (colour versus shape) trial-by-trial under speed, indexing set-shifting efficiency
inhibitory_control_attention: incongruent cards create a Stroop-like conflict between dimensions that must be suppressed
response_inhibition_impulse_control: on rare lock trials the child must withhold the sort
attention_control: monitoring the rule banner and sustaining focus across a fast block
one_liner: The child sorts each card fast by the rule the banner shows - sometimes by colour, sometimes by shape - and must freeze when a lock icon appears.
interaction: A card (a coloured shape) drops in the centre and a small banner shows the current rule (a paint-drop for colour or an outline for shape); the child taps the LEFT or RIGHT bin that matches the card on the cued dimension. The rule switches unpredictably between cards, and on incongruent cards the two dimensions point to different bins. On rare lock trials the child must withhold the sort. Switches, conflicts and withholds are logged; the block is speeded. No typing; the rule is shown as an icon and read aloud.
self_teach: The ghost-hand sees the paint-drop banner and sorts a red star into the red bin, then the banner flips to the shape icon and it sorts the next card by its shape - under 10s, showing watch the banner to know the rule, freeze on the lock. One unscored warm-up of slow single-rule sorts runs before the fast switching block begins.

learning_science.why: Switching the active sorting rule trial-by-trial produces switch costs that index the speed of reconfiguring task set.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Unpredictable colour and shape rule switches yield a switch-cost metric while maintained accuracy is required.
learning_science.source: Diamond, A. (2013). Executive functions. Annual Review of Psychology 64.

learning_science.why: Incongruent cards create a Stroop-like conflict between dimensions that must be suppressed to sort correctly.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Congruent versus incongruent cards give an interference-cost signal and lock trials add response inhibition.
learning_science.source: MacLeod, C. M. (1991). Half a century of research on the Stroop effect: An integrative review. Psychological Bulletin 109(2).

tail_precision_rationale: M-SWITCHCOST (switch-minus-repeat RT) and M-PERSEV (sorting by the just-abandoned rule) isolate set-shifting efficiency, M-CONGEFF isolates interference control, and M-COMM isolates withholding, so a child who holds speed, flexibility and accuracy together separates cleanly. M-RTVAR and M-COMBO ensure consistency and accuracy-gated speed drive the estimate rather than impulsive peak speed.
age_rationale: Sorting a card into one of two big bins by a shown icon is accessible from K-1 (the border/advanced DCCS switch task is validated in early childhood) with slow pacing and rare switches. 2-3 and 4-5 add incongruent cards and occasional locks; 6-8 gets fast pacing, frequent switches and interference that separate flexible controllers. Icons are read aloud; no reading.

adaptive.content_range: slow single-rule sorts (K-1) up to fast frequent-switch incongruent sorting with locks (6-8)
adaptive.notes: Card streams are procedurally generated with parametric switch and congruency rates; flexibility compresses at the very top so this profiles control alongside high-tail reasoning.

engagement_hook: A speedy sort-the-card game where the rule keeps flipping and locks make you freeze keeps children alert, with a combo for clean fast streaks.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Large bins and per-band pacing keep it a control task not a motor race; cards carry both colour and shape so colour-vision alone is not required; anticipatory taps under 150 ms flagged; M-COMBO gates speed on accuracy; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty.

name: Coin Market
topics_techniques_covered: symbolic_magnitude_arithmetic: the child compares symbolic price magnitudes (which toy costs more) across close and far pairs
place_value_composition: the child pays exact prices by composing amounts from ones and ten-bills, regrouping ten ones into a ten
problem_solving: make exact amounts and choose larger magnitudes under a deadline, a numeric constraint-satisfaction task
one_liner: The child pays exact prices with coins and ten-bills and taps which of two toys costs more, building quantities from ones and tens.
interaction: Two modes advance a shopping trip: (1) a price tag is shown and the child taps coins (ones) and ten-bills into a pay tray to make exactly that amount, regrouping ten ones into a ten when helpful; (2) two toys with price tags appear and the child taps the one that costs more. Correct answers stock the shelf. Numerals are read aloud on tap for pre-readers. No typing.
self_teach: The ghost-hand sees a price of 13, taps one ten-bill and three ones into the tray which turns green, then taps the pricier of two toys which sparkles - under 10s, showing build the exact price, then pick the bigger price. One unscored warm-up (pay a price of 3 with ones) runs before scored adaptive items begin.

learning_science.why: Money is a canonical base-ten context where flexible composition and regrouping predict arithmetic competence.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The pay mode scores regrouping strategy (one ten plus three ones over thirteen ones), targeting place-value understanding not calculation fluency.
learning_science.source: Fuson, K. C. (1990). Conceptual structures for multidigit numbers. Cognition and Instruction 7(4).

learning_science.principle: Symbolic magnitude comparison and math ability
learning_science.why: The speed and accuracy of comparing symbolic magnitudes is a robust correlate of math achievement.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The compare mode uses price magnitudes across close and far pairs with a deadline to index symbolic magnitude processing.
learning_science.source: De Smedt, B., Noel, M.-P., Gilmore, C., & Ansari, D. (2013). The relationship between symbolic and non-symbolic magnitude processing and math achievement. Trends in Neuroscience and Education 2(2).

tail_precision_rationale: M-EFF on the pay mode credits efficient regrouping (fewest coins and bills, using tens over many ones) that marks flexible place-value reasoners, and M-ERRTYPE distinguishes a magnitude near-miss from a place-value slip (a tens and ones swap). M-SPEEDACC ensures fast comparisons are credited only when accurate and M-PATH preserves the coin-placement sequence for strategy scoring.
age_rationale: Paying small prices with ones and picking the bigger of two prices is accessible in K-1 with read-aloud numerals. 2-3 introduces two-digit prices and regrouping; 4-5 and 6-8 add three-digit amounts, tighter magnitude pairs and deadlines. Tap-only input and audio numerals keep literacy and motor load low.

adaptive.content_range: one-digit pay and easy compares (K-1) up to three-digit regrouping and close-magnitude compares under deadline (6-8 tail)
difficulty_levers: magnitude closeness of the compare pair
adaptive.notes: Prices are procedurally generated with an auto-checked minimal-coin key for M-EFF and matched compare pairs for parallel forms.

engagement_hook: Running a toy shop by paying exact prices and spotting the pricier toy is a familiar pretend-play hook that keeps young children engaged.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Read-aloud numerals remove reading load; coins and bills are large tap targets removing motor demands; audio is replayable and captioned for accessibility; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; M-SPEEDACC prevents rewarding impulsive fast-wrong comparisons.

name: Number Balance
topics_techniques_covered: symbolic_magnitude_arithmetic: the child compares and combines numeric magnitudes so a pan balance reads level, and picks the heavier loaded pan
place_value_composition: the child composes a target by adding ten-blocks and ones, regrouping ten ones into a ten to balance
problem_solving: reach equilibrium (or a missing-addend balance) under block constraints, a numeric constraint-satisfaction task
one_liner: The child hangs number-blocks on a pan balance so both sides weigh the same, comparing and composing magnitudes until the beam is level.
interaction: A pan balance tips toward the heavier side; one pan may already hold a number or target. The child taps ones-blocks and ten-blocks into the empty pan to make it balance, regrouping ten ones into a ten, and the beam tilts live as they add. When both sides are equal the beam locks level. In compare rounds two loaded pans appear and the child taps the heavier side. Numerals are read aloud on tap. No typing.
self_teach: The ghost-hand sees a 12 on the left pan, taps one ten-block and two ones onto the right pan and the beam swings level and glows - under 10s, showing add blocks until it balances. One unscored warm-up (balance a 3) runs before scored adaptive items begin.

learning_science.why: Making both sides equal builds a relational meaning of equals (balance) rather than an operational one (compute the total), a known early separator of algebra-ready reasoning.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The balance beam frames equality as a relation so the child must equate magnitudes, and the first placement reveals relational versus operational thinking.
learning_science.source: McNeil, N. M., & Alibali, M. W. (2005). Knowledge change as a function of mathematics experience: All contexts are not created equal. Journal of Cognition and Development 6(2).

learning_science.why: Composing a target from tens and ones flexibly predicts arithmetic competence.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Balancing rewards regrouping (a ten plus two ones over twelve ones) so place-value strategy is scored.
learning_science.source: Fuson, K. C. (1990). Conceptual structures for multidigit numbers. Cognition and Instruction 7(4).

tail_precision_rationale: M-EQREL flags whether the child treats equals relationally (balances both sides) or operationally (dumps ones), a research-backed early separator that dichotomous accuracy hides. M-EFF credits efficient regrouped balancing and M-ERRTYPE distinguishes a magnitude miss from a place-value slip, concentrating information where pre-algebraic talent emerges.
age_rationale: Adding blocks until a beam balances and picking the heavier pan is accessible in K-1 with small numbers and read-aloud numerals. 2-3 adds two-digit balancing and regrouping; 4-5 and 6-8 add larger numbers, missing-addend balancing and non-canonical targets. Tap-only input and audio numerals keep literacy and motor load low.

adaptive.content_range: balance small single-digit weights (K-1) up to two and three-digit regrouped and missing-addend balancing (6-8 tail)
adaptive.notes: Targets are procedurally generated with a minimal-block key for M-EFF and non-canonical framings for M-EQREL.

engagement_hook: The seesaw swing of the beam tipping and then locking level gives immediate, playful feedback that makes balancing numbers feel like a physical game.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Read-aloud numerals remove reading load; large blocks remove motor demands; the live beam makes the equality outcome unambiguous; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; M-SPEEDACC prevents rewarding impulsive fast-wrong balancing.

name: Fib Finder
topics_techniques_covered: listening_comprehension_inference: the child listens to a short spoken argument and infers whether the conclusion follows and where it breaks, scored on the inference depth caught
verbal_reasoning_argumentation: the child evaluates a claim-and-reason and locates the unsupported step or false premise
verbal_absurdities: at easy levels the child spots an impossible or foolish statement in the spoken passage
one_liner: The child listens to a short spoken reason-and-claim and taps the part that does not make sense or the step that does not follow.
interaction: A character speaks a two or three line argument (for example, all birds can fly, so a penguin can fly to the tree). The scene shows two to three tappable picture cards, each standing for one spoken statement or the conclusion; the child taps the card that is wrong or does not follow. A REPLAY button re-plays the audio. The correct choice lights up. Difficulty scales from silly absurdities to subtle logical gaps. No reading; all statements are spoken with picture cues.
self_teach: The ghost-hand listens to a fish riding a bicycle to school, then taps the fish-on-bicycle card which shakes as silly - under 10s, showing tap the part that cannot be true. One unscored warm-up on an obvious absurdity runs before scored, subtler flawed-reasoning items begin.

learning_science.why: Mature verbal reasoning evaluates whether a conclusion actually follows from its reasons rather than only agreeing with it.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The child must locate the unsupported step or false premise, so the score reflects argument evaluation not opinion.
learning_science.source: Kuhn, D. (1991). The Skills of Argument. Cambridge University Press.

learning_science.principle: Listening comprehension in the Simple View of Reading
learning_science.why: Delivering the argument by ear isolates language comprehension and inference from decoding ability.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Full audio with picture cards lets pre-readers show comprehension and flaw detection.
learning_science.source: Gough, P. B., & Tunmer, W. E. (1986). Decoding, reading, and reading disability. Remedial and Special Education 7(1).

tail_precision_rationale: M-INFDEPTH (deepest flaw layer detected: impossible fact, then invalid inference, then subtle unsupported warrant) is the sharpest tail separator because verbal-reasoning discrimination is about how subtle a gap a child can catch. M-LURETYPE reads whether errors are pulled by the plausible-but-irrelevant statement and M-HINT (replays) adds a dynamic-assessment signal.
age_rationale: Spotting an obvious spoken absurdity with picture cards is accessible from 2-3. 4-5 adds simple does-not-follow reasoning; 6-8 adds subtle unsupported warrants and near-valid arguments that separate strong verbal reasoners. Audio delivery with picture cards means no reading at any band.

adaptive.content_range: obvious absurdities (2-3) up to subtle unsupported-warrant arguments (6-8 tail)
adaptive.notes: Argument skeletons are templated with flaw-type-tagged statements and lure classes; new spoken lines need audio generation so cloning is moderate.

engagement_hook: Playing a fib-catching detective who spots the silly or sneaky part of what a character says makes critical listening feel like a game.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Full audio plus picture cards removes reading load; replays are logged as hint use not blocked; flaws are designed by type not trickery; topics are kept culturally neutral so background knowledge does not confound reasoning; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty.

name: Best Because
topics_techniques_covered: verbal_reasoning_argumentation: the child selects the reason that best supports a claim and later gives the counter-reason, scored on claim-reason link quality
listening_comprehension_inference: the child comprehends a spoken claim and reasons and infers which link is strongest
one_liner: The child hears a claim and taps the one reason, from several, that best supports it - supplying the missing because that bridges reason to conclusion.
interaction: A spoken claim appears (for example, we should bring umbrellas today) with two to four picture reason cards spoken aloud on tap (dark clouds; it is Tuesday; the grass is green). The child taps the reason that best supports the claim; a strength meter fills by how well the reason links to the claim. Later items ask the child to also tap which reason a rival would give against the claim. A REPLAY button re-plays audio. No reading; picture-plus-audio cards.
self_teach: The ghost-hand hears we should bring umbrellas and taps the dark-clouds card which powers a full strength bar, skipping the green-grass card which stays dim - under 10s, showing pick the reason that really supports the claim. One unscored warm-up with one strong and one clearly unrelated reason runs before scored, subtler items begin.

learning_science.why: A strong argument links a claim to data through a warrant, and recognising the best supporting link is core argumentation skill.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Reason cards are tagged by link strength (strong warrant, weak, irrelevant) so the choice is scored against argument structure not surface agreement.
learning_science.source: Toulmin, S. E. (1958). The Uses of Argument. Cambridge University Press.

learning_science.principle: Listening comprehension in the Simple View of Reading
learning_science.why: Spoken claims and reasons isolate reasoning from decoding for pre-readers.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Audio-plus-picture delivery lets young and emerging readers show argument evaluation.
learning_science.source: Gough, P. B., & Tunmer, W. E. (1986). Decoding, reading, and reading disability. Remedial and Special Education 7(1).

tail_precision_rationale: M-POLY (graded strength of the chosen reason) extracts several bits of tail information from one item and M-LURETYPE reveals whether errors are pulled by thematic-associate or weak-but-related reasons, grading discrimination of evidential relevance. M-INFDEPTH tracks whether the child also supplies the counter-reason (a deeper argument layer) and M-RTFIRST separates deliberate evaluation from surface matching.
age_rationale: Choosing the obviously supporting reason for a concrete claim with picture-plus-audio cards is accessible from 2-3. 4-5 adds weak-but-related lures; 6-8 adds abstract claims, subtle relevance differences and the counter-reason step that separate strong verbal reasoners. Audio and picture cards mean no reading at any band.

adaptive.content_range: one-strong-one-unrelated concrete claims (2-3) up to abstract claims with subtle relevance lures and a counter-reason step (6-8 tail)
difficulty_levers: requirement to also give the counter-reason
adaptive.notes: Claim and reason sets are templated with relevance-tagged cards and lure classes; spoken lines need audio so cloning is moderate.

engagement_hook: Powering up a claim with the strongest reason and watching a strength bar fill turns argument-building into a satisfying duel of reasons.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Picture-plus-audio cards keep reading load low; tap-to-choose removes typing; cards are tagged by link role so scoring reflects relevance not opinion; topics are kept culturally neutral; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty.

name: Letter Climb
topics_techniques_covered: orthographic_lexical_access: the child changes one letter at a time to climb from a start word to a goal word, each rung a real word, indexing rapid access to the orthographic lexicon and word neighbourhoods
one_liner: The child changes one letter at a time to climb from the start word to the goal word, each rung a real word.
interaction: A start word (for example CAT) and a length-matched goal word are shown as letter tiles; the child taps a letter position then taps a new letter to change exactly one letter, forming the next word, which must be a real word (valid words lock in as a rung; invalid strings gently shake). The ladder grows until the goal is reached in as few rungs as possible. Letters are voiced on tap. No keyboard typing.
self_teach: The ghost-hand turns CAT into COT by changing one letter, which locks as a rung, then COT into COG - under 10s, showing change one letter to make a new word and climb. One unscored warm-up (one change reaches the goal) runs before scored ladders begin.

learning_science.why: Finding a valid neighbour word by a single letter change requires rapid access to the orthographic lexicon, a strong verbal-ability marker.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Each rung must be a real word, so the task indexes orthographic-lexical access and neighbourhood knowledge not handwriting.
learning_science.source: Ehri, L. C. (2005). Learning to read words: Theory, findings, and issues. Scientific Studies of Reading 9(2).

learning_science.principle: Search efficiency in a constrained word space
learning_science.why: Reaching the goal in few rungs rewards planful lexical search over random letter changes.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Rungs-over-minimum is scored so efficient lexical pathfinding is credited.
learning_science.source: Newell, A., & Simon, H. A. (1972). Human Problem Solving. Prentice-Hall.

tail_precision_rationale: M-EFF (rungs versus the shortest ladder) is a continuous ceiling-resistant separator of lexical pathfinding and M-VOCABLVL captures the rarity of the intermediate words a child can access. M-RTFIRST and inter-rung latency index lexical-access speed while M-PATH preserves the full ladder for strategy scoring.
age_rationale: Changing one letter to make a new word needs emerging spelling and decoding, so it starts at 4-5 with short high-frequency three-letter ladders and letter audio. 6-8 uses longer words, longer minimum ladders and rarer intermediate words that reward deep lexical access. Below 4-5 letter-word knowledge is generally insufficient, setting the floor.

adaptive.content_range: short three-letter one-change ladders (4-5) up to longer words with long minimum ladders and rare rungs (6-8 tail)
adaptive.notes: Ladders are generated against a frequency-tagged lexicon with a shortest-path solver for M-EFF and M-VOCABLVL and unlimited parallel forms.

engagement_hook: Climbing a word ladder one letter at a time toward the goal word is a classic puzzle with fewest-rungs stars that reward clever routes.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Letters are voiced on tap so decoding does not block emerging readers; tap-to-change removes handwriting and keyboard load; the validated lexicon accepts legitimate rare words; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; rung efficiency and breadth not raw speed are scored.

name: Word Trace
topics_techniques_covered: orthographic_lexical_access: the child traces paths through a grid of neighbouring letters to produce as many valid words as possible under time, indexing lexical-access speed, breadth and orthographic knowledge
one_liner: The child traces paths through a grid of neighbouring letters to spell as many real words as they can before the timer runs out.
interaction: A grid of letter tiles is shown; the child drags or taps a chain of adjacent letters to spell a word then lifts or taps ENTER; valid words score and animate onto a shelf while invalid chains gently clear. Longer and rarer words earn brighter gems. A visible sand timer bounds the round. Letters are voiced on tap. No keyboard typing (trace-to-build only).
self_teach: The ghost-hand traces C-A-T across three touching tiles and the word flies to the shelf with a chime, then traces C-A-R-T for a bigger gem - under 10s, showing connect touching letters to make words, longer is better. One unscored warm-up on an easy grid runs before the scored, timed round begins.

learning_science.why: Finding words hidden in a letter grid demands fast, broad access to the orthographic lexicon.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Scoring rewards the number, length and rarity of valid traced words under time, indexing lexical access and breadth not spelling dictation.
learning_science.source: Ehri, L. C. (2005). Learning to read words: Theory, findings, and issues. Scientific Studies of Reading 9(2).

learning_science.principle: Productive fluency as an ability signal
learning_science.why: Open production over selection lowers the ceiling and reveals verbal breadth.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The child produces as many words as possible so fluency and lexical depth separate the tail; letter audio lowers the decoding barrier.
learning_science.source: Carroll, J. B. (1993). Human Cognitive Abilities: A Survey of Factor-Analytic Studies. Cambridge University Press.

tail_precision_rationale: M-IDEAFLU (distinct valid words found) and M-VOCABLVL (rarest word-frequency band produced) are ceiling-resistant fluency and lexical-depth signals that keep separating strong verbal children after short common words are exhausted. M-RTFIRST (time to first word) indexes lexical-access speed and M-FLEX (variety of word lengths and roots) distinguishes deep lexicons from repetitive stems.
age_rationale: Tracing short words in a small grid with letter audio starts at 4-5 once basic letter-sound knowledge emerges. 6-8 uses larger grids that afford long and rare words and tighter timers that reward deep lexical access. Trace-to-build avoids handwriting and keyboard demands. Below 4-5 letter knowledge is generally insufficient, setting the floor.

adaptive.content_range: small grids affording short words (4-5) up to large grids affording long and rare words under tight time (6-8 tail)
difficulty_levers: letter distribution (how many long and rare words afforded)
adaptive.notes: Grids are generated against a frequency-tagged lexicon that enumerates the valid word set for M-IDEAFLU and M-VOCABLVL and gives matched parallel forms.

engagement_hook: Racing a sand timer to trace as many words as possible from a grid, chasing bright gems for long rare words, drives effortful production.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Letters are voiced on tap so decoding does not block emerging readers; trace-to-build removes handwriting and keyboard load; the validated lexicon avoids penalising legitimate rare words; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; breadth and rarity over raw speed are scored.

name: Tone Detective
topics_techniques_covered: empathy_emotion_recognition: the child identifies the emotion from a speaker's tone of voice (vocal/prosodic emotion recognition) and gauges its intensity, scoring empathic accuracy and calibration
one_liner: The child listens to the same sentence said in different feelings and taps the emotion that matches the speaker's tone of voice.
interaction: A neutral sentence (for example, oh, it is you) is played in an emotional tone of voice while a plain character is shown. The child taps the matching emotion from icon buttons (happy, sad, angry, scared, surprised, calm) then sets an intensity slider (a little to a lot). A REPLAY button re-plays the clip. Empathic accuracy, intensity calibration and confusions are logged. Emotion buttons are icon-based with audio labels; no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand hears a bright, giggly tone, taps the happy button and slides intensity high while the character beams - under 10s, showing listen to how it is said, then pick the feeling. One unscored warm-up on a clearly happy tone runs before scored, subtler tones begin.

learning_science.why: Reading affect from tone of voice is a distinct, measurable channel of emotion recognition beyond facial cues.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Items vary tone with fixed neutral words so the score reflects prosodic emotion decoding not word content.
learning_science.source: Banse, R., & Scherer, K. R. (1996). Acoustic profiles in vocal emotion expression. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 70(3).

learning_science.why: Judging emotion intensity and not just its label indexes empathic calibration.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The intensity slider yields calibration between chosen and true intensity, adding signal beyond the label.
learning_science.source: Ickes, W. (1993). Empathic accuracy. Journal of Personality 61(4).

tail_precision_rationale: M-POLY (graded intensity-calibration score) turns each clip into a fine-grained signal that avoids the ceiling of basic-emotion labelling and M-CONF captures calibration between chosen intensity and the true tone. M-ERRTYPE reads which confusable emotion (fear versus surprise, anger versus sadness) is mistaken so subtle tones separate highly empathic children.
age_rationale: Matching a clearly happy or sad tone to an icon is accessible from 2-3 with audio labels. 4-5 adds fear and surprise and coarse intensity; 6-8 adds subtle and blended tones and fine intensity calibration that separate advanced social listeners. All input is tap and slide with audio so no reading is needed.

adaptive.content_range: clearly happy or sad tones (2-3) up to subtle blended tones with fine intensity (6-8 tail)
adaptive.notes: Clips are parameterised prosody sets with graded intensity for M-POLY; subtle tones and diverse voices need curation so cloning is moderate; include diverse voices to avoid own-group bias.

engagement_hook: Being a detective who cracks how someone really feels from their voice is a warm hook that elicits genuine emotion reading.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Icon buttons plus audio labels remove reading load; tap and slide input removes motor precision demands; use diverse voices to avoid own-group bias; replays are logged not blocked; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; scoring credits calibrated intensity over a single label.

name: How Do They Feel?
topics_techniques_covered: empathy_emotion_recognition: the child infers a character's emotion from a social situation (situational/theory-of-mind emotion inference, no face shown) and chooses an apt helping response, scoring empathic accuracy and calibration
one_liner: The child watches a short social situation and infers how the character feels from what happens, then picks the kind thing to do.
interaction: A brief narrated animation shows a social situation (a child's tower is knocked over; a friend shares a snack). No face is shown at the key moment; the child must infer the feeling from the events and tap the matching emotion icon, rate how strong it is, then tap which of two to three actions would help most. A REPLAY button re-plays the scene. Inference accuracy, intensity calibration and response choice are logged. Icons with audio labels; no reading.
self_teach: The ghost-hand watches a tower get knocked down, taps the sad button (no face was shown), slides intensity up, then taps the help-rebuild action which cheers the character - under 10s, showing think how they feel from what happened, then help. One unscored warm-up on an obvious situation runs before scored, subtler ones begin.

learning_science.principle: Theory of mind and situational emotion inference
learning_science.why: Inferring emotion from a situation rather than a face taps perspective-taking and social causal reasoning, a deeper social-cognition skill.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The key emotion is hidden from the face so the child must infer it from events, isolating situational empathy.
learning_science.source: Wellman, H. M., Cross, D., & Watson, J. (2001). Meta-analysis of theory-of-mind development: The truth about false belief. Child Development 72(3).

learning_science.why: Choosing an apt helping action indexes whether emotion understanding translates into appropriate social response.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The response-choice step scores context-appropriate helping beyond the emotion label.
learning_science.source: Ickes, W. (1993). Empathic accuracy. Journal of Personality 61(4).

tail_precision_rationale: M-INFDEPTH (literal event, then felt-emotion inference, then predicted reaction, then best helping response) captures how deep a social inference the child reaches, the sharpest tail separator. M-POLY and M-CONF grade intensity calibration and M-ERRTYPE reads which situational misread (missing the cause, wrong valence) occurs so subtle scenes separate strong social reasoners.
age_rationale: Inferring a clear feeling from an obvious situation and picking a helpful action is accessible from 2-3 with narration and icons. 4-5 adds less obvious situations and intensity; 6-8 adds mixed feelings, misleading context and subtler helping choices that separate advanced perspective-takers. Narration and icons mean no reading at any band.

adaptive.content_range: obvious situations with one clear feeling (2-3) up to mixed-feeling scenes with misleading context and subtle responses (6-8 tail)
difficulty_levers: number of emotion and action options
adaptive.notes: Scenes are templated social situations with depth-tagged probes; new narrations need audio so cloning is moderate; include diverse characters to avoid own-group bias.

engagement_hook: Figuring out how a character feels from a little story and choosing how to help feels like caring for a friend, eliciting authentic empathy.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Narration plus icon options removes reading load; tap and slide input removes motor demands; scenes are culturally neutral with diverse characters to avoid bias; replays are logged not blocked; ghost-hand plus warm-up controls novelty; calibrated intensity and apt response are credited over a single label.
